questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{3}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-{(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =3({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{3})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=1\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{8}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{8}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=xy(1-{x}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot (1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
